title: Leaving radio in 1962 to work for Ebony Magazine
summary: A friend at the Urban League recommends him; Ben Wright calls from New York, flies him up, and he is tried out on market research.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Yeah. Yeah. It's a new day. It's a new day. Okay, where were we? Okay, so after, I mean after the Sentinel, where, what other, did you work for another paper after that?

No, I did not. What I did, I stayed in radio until 1962. And I got a call from a friend of mine by the name of Dorsey who was working for the Urban League at that time. Ebony Magazine had a position open, and for some reason Dorsey picked me over whomever at the time. And to make a long story short, I came back and I talked to my wife. And my wife said, well, find out what they're paying and so forth and so on. And after all, we're gonna have a family and we need a little extra money. So I said, well, I can keep this and do this on the weekend. And I still work for Ebony Magazine. So I told Dorsey, okay. Well, what Dorsey did, Dorsey called New York. And Ben Wright, who was my immediate supervisor at the time, he called me long distance. I didn't know who he was. I said, hello? He said, I'm Ben Wright. I said, glad to know you. I said, where are you calling from? He said, I'm calling from New York. He said, I understand you're supposed to be coming to work for us. I said, who are you? He said, I'm Ben Wright. I'm with Ebony Magazine. I said, well, you didn't say that at first. Well, we had a conversation going, all right. So eventually, he said, well, look, Tex, I'm gonna send you plane fare and money's to travel to New York. So they sent me a package, nice package. Come to New York. I told my wife, I said, I'm going to New York. I'm gonna check them out. So Ebony put me to work with McCann, Erickson, and a couple of these other white firms to see if I had the background to work with them. Because they were already handling business for these major corporations. So I worked with them on certain assignments to do market research. I did all right. I won the Wright Fowler Award back then in 1962. I was so good, I felt proud of myself.

So what was that award? Explain that award. That was an award for promotion. In other words, when you would call on somebody like Macy's, or you'd call on the Falstead Brewing Company, and if, in other words, they would, what you call, they would monitor you. And then the boss would call and say, how did my new representative appear to you? Did you like his professional approach and this, that, and the other? Yeah. So everywhere I went, I got less than 95. On 20 major calls in and around New York, everything I got was 95 to 100. I said I like his demeanor. I like his presentation. I like his style. I like his vocal rhythm, or whatever they were saying about me. Yeah. You know, it made me feel very good. I said, hell, you mean to tell me I'm big time in New York? How about that?
